text: "Now you, son of man, take a brick, set it in front of you, and engrave on it a city — Jerusalem.
Lay siege against it: build a siege wall, throw up a ramp, set up camps, and place battering rams around it.

Then take an iron griddle and set it up as an iron wall between you and the city. Set your face toward it; it shall be under siege, and you yourself shall besiege it. This is a sign for the house of Israel.

versions.text: Then take an iron griddle and set it up as an iron wall between you and the city. Turn your face toward it, so that it is under siege, and press the siege against it. This is a sign for the house of Israel.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has three successive clauses (set your face / it shall be under siege / you shall besiege it) rather than a purpose clause. "so that it is under siege, and press the siege against it" is redundant when read aloud; the revision keeps the sequence and avoids repeating "siege" as both noun and verb in the same breath.

text: "Then lie down on your left side and lay the guilt of the house of Israel upon that side. For as many days as you lie on that side, you shall bear their guilt.

versions.text: "Then lie down on your left side and lay the guilt of the house of Israel upon it. For as many days as you lie on that side, you shall bear their guilt.
versions.explanation: In oral reading "upon it" has no clear antecedent (the hearer may take it as the brick of verse 1). Making the referent explicit ("that side") matches the Hebrew suffix, which refers back to the side on which he lies.

text: I have assigned you the years of their guilt as a number of days: three hundred and ninety days. So you shall bear the guilt of the house of Israel.
When you have finished these, lie down again, this time on your right side, and bear the guilt of the house of Judah forty days. I have assigned you one day for each year.
Set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem, with your arm bared, and prophesy against it.
And see, I am putting ropes on you so that you cannot turn from one side to the other until you have completed the days of your siege.

"Take wheat and barley, beans and lentils, millet and spelt; put them in a single vessel and make them into bread for yourself. You shall eat it during the number of days you lie on your side — three hundred and ninety days.
The food you eat shall be weighed out, twenty shekels a day; you shall eat it at set times.
And you shall drink water by measure, a sixth of a hin; you shall drink it at set times.
You shall eat it as a barley cake, baking it in their sight over human excrement."
And the LORD said, "This is how the people of Israel shall eat their bread — unclean — among the nations where I will drive them."
Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! I have never defiled myself. From my youth until now I have never eaten anything that died of itself or was torn by beasts, and no tainted meat has ever entered my mouth."
He said to me, "See, I allow you cow dung instead of human dung; you may prepare your bread over that."
Then he said to me, "Son of man, I am about to break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. They shall eat bread by weight and in anxiety, and drink water by measure and in horror,
so that, lacking bread and water, they will be appalled, each man with his brother, and waste away in their guilt."

versions.text: so that, lacking bread and water, they will look at one another in dismay and waste away in their guilt."
versions.explanation: The verb here means "be appalled/desolate," not "look at"; the current rendering adds an act of looking that is not in the Hebrew. The suggested wording keeps the idiom "each man and his brother" and still reads smoothly aloud.
